meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Perhaps all the dragons in our lives are princesses who are only waiting to see us act, just once, with beauty and courage'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Rilke: eighth letter to Franz Xaver Kappus, 12 August 1904. The English everyone quotes is Stephen Mitchell's 1984 translation, not Rilke's words.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Rilke wrote this in the eighth of his Letters to a Young Poet, sent to the cadet Franz Xaver Kappus from Borgeby gård in Sweden on 12 August 1904 and first published in German in 1929. The exact English wording quoted everywhere — “act, just once, with beauty and courage” — is Stephen Mitchell’s 1984 translation, confirmed in the Random House edition; earlier English versions word it differently.

docMeta.dd: Briefe an einen jungen Dichter (Letters to a Young Poet)
Eighth letter to Franz Xaver Kappus — Borgeby gård, Flädie, Sweden, 12 August 1904
Stephen Mitchell, Random House, 1984 — the source of the exact English wording

source.excerpt: Wie sollten wir jener alten Mythen vergessen können, die am Anfange aller Völker stehen, der Mythen von den Drachen, die sich im äußersten Augenblick in Prinzessinnen verwandeln; vielleicht sind alle Drachen unseres Lebens Prinzessinnen, die nur darauf warten, uns einmal schön und mutig zu sehen. Vielleicht ist alles Schreckliche im tiefsten Grunde das Hilflose, das von uns Hilfe will.
trail: The German original sits in the eighth letter, headed Borgeby gård, Flädie, Schweden, am 12. August 1904: “vielleicht sind alle Drachen unseres Lebens Prinzessinnen, die nur darauf warten, uns einmal schön und mutig zu sehen.” Read the letter ↗
The book itself is posthumous: Kappus sent the letters to Rilke’s daughter in 1929 and they appeared that year from Insel-Verlag in Leipzig, as number 406 of the Insel-Bücherei. Publication history ↗

M. D. Herter Norton’s English translates the passage “perhaps all the dragons of our lives are princesses who are only waiting to see us once beautiful and brave” — close in sense, nothing like the wording that circulates. Norton’s full text ↗

A full-text search of scanned books places the exact string “act, just once, with beauty and courage” in the Random House 1984, Vintage 1986 and Modern Library 2001 printings of the letters — all Stephen Mitchell’s translation. The 1984 edition ↗

author.name: Rainer Maria Rilke
author.heading: Who Rilke was
author.metaLine: 1875–1926 · Austrian poet & novelist, writing in German and French
author.bio: Rainer Maria Rilke was born in Prague in 1875 and died in Switzerland in 1926, and is one of the most widely read poets of the German language — author of the Duino Elegies, the Sonnets to Orpheus and the novel The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge. Between 1903 and 1908 he answered ten letters from Franz Xaver Kappus, a teenage officer cadet at the Theresian Military Academy who had asked whether his poems were any good. Rilke mostly declined to judge the poems and wrote instead about solitude, patience and the uses of difficulty — letters that Kappus published in 1929, three years after Rilke’s death, and which became Rilke’s most-read book.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost when it travels
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare famous quotes that survives checking. The attribution is right; what goes wrong is the wording, because Rilke wrote in German and the sentence people post is a particular translator’s English.

items.why: “Act, just once, with beauty and courage” is Mitchell’s phrasing, published in his translation of the letters by Random House in 1984 and reissued by Vintage and the Modern Library. Rilke’s German is “uns einmal schön und mutig zu sehen” — literally, to see us beautiful and brave, just once. Quoting the English as Rilke’s own words drops the translator who made them. The 1984 Random House edition ↗

The older Norton translation renders the same sentence “perhaps all the dragons of our lives are princesses who are only waiting to see us once beautiful and brave” — of our lives, not in, and no “act, just once.” Hybrid versions mixing the two circulate widely. Norton’s text ↗

Most reposts give no work at all, and some file it under Rilke’s poetry. It is prose, from a letter: the eighth of ten replies to Franz Xaver Kappus, written at Borgeby gård in Sweden on 12 August 1904. Dates of all ten letters ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Rilke really wrote it — in German, to a young officer cadet, on 12 August 1904 ↗. The English you have seen belongs to his translator.

context.heading: Why he wrote it
lead: Kappus had written to Rilke about a run of sadnesses he could not shake. Rilke’s reply — the eighth letter, written from a Swedish country house in August 1904 — is an argument that the frightening things in a life are not intruders but arrivals: that sadness is the moment something new enters us, and that what we call destiny “goes forth from within people, not from without into them.”

The dragons sentence is the turn of that argument. Rilke reaches for the oldest fairy tales, the ones in which the monster changes shape at the last second, and offers them not as consolation but as instruction: the terrible thing may be waiting on us, not the other way round. He follows it immediately with a line about everything frightening being, at bottom, something helpless that wants our help.
detailsBody: Rilke died in December 1926. In 1929 Kappus sent the letters to Rilke’s daughter Ruth, and she and Rilke’s widow Clara Westhoff published the ten replies with a preface by Kappus, as number 406 of the Insel-Bücherei.
The original manuscripts of Rilke’s letters were auctioned off by Kappus in 1953 and their present whereabouts are not known; Kappus’s own letters survive in the Rilke archive at Gernsbach.
context.pull: Rilke is not saying the dragons are harmless. He is saying they are waiting to see what you do.

sourcesVerified.claim: The German text of Rilke's eighth letter, headed Borgeby gård, Flädie, Schweden, am 12. August 1904, contains "vielleicht sind alle Drachen unseres Lebens Prinzessinnen, die nur darauf warten, uns einmal schön und mutig zu sehen."

M. D. Herter Norton's English translation, in the letter headed "EIGHT / Borgeby gard, Fladie, Sweden, August 12th, 1904", reads "perhaps all the dragons of our lives are princesses who are only waiting to see us once beautiful and brave" — a different wording from the popular one.
Internet Archive record for Letters to a Young Poet, New York: Random House, 1984, with associated name Mitchell, Stephen, 1943- (i.e. the Stephen Mitchell translation).

Full-text search of scanned books returns the exact strings "all the dragons in our lives are princesses who are only waiting" and "act, just once, with beauty and courage" inside the Random House 1984, Vintage 1986 and Modern Library 2001 editions of Letters to a Young Poet (all the Mitchell translation).

Briefe an einen jungen Dichter was first published in 1929 by Insel Verlag as number 406 of the Insel-Bücherei; the eighth letter was written at Borgeby gård (Flädie, Sweden) on 12 August 1904; Kappus sent the letters to Rilke's daughter Ruth in 1929 and the manuscripts were auctioned in 1953.

Rainer Maria Rilke, 4 December 1875 – 29 December 1926, Austrian poet writing in German and French; Franz Xaver Kappus (1883–1966) was a 19-year-old officer cadet at the Theresian Military Academy when the correspondence began, and published the ten letters in 1929.
Internet Archive holds a scanned Insel-Verlag (Leipzig) German edition of Rilke's Briefe an einen jungen Dichter.
